extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, safety_data_sheet preparers, hazard_classifiers, laboratory and regulatory compliance professionals
extracted.subtask_short: hazard classification for chemicals and mixtures
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for classifying substances and mixtures under physical and target-organ/aspiration hazard classes (GHS-aligned/OSHA HCS Appendix criteria), including thresholds, test references, and bridging principles for mixtures when mixture-level data are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reliable human/animal evidence and weight-of-evidence for mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: When reliable and good quality evidence from human experience or appropriate studies in experimental animals... is available for the mixture, then the mixture shall be classified by weight of evidence evaluation of these data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care shall be exercised in evaluating data on mixtures, that the dose, duration, observation or analysis, do not render the results inconclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principles for classifying untested mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the mixture itself has not been tested... but there are sufficient data on both the individual ingredients and similar tested mixtures to adequately characterize the hazards of the mixture, these data shall be used in accordance with the following bridging principles: Dilution; Batching; Concentration of mixtures; Interpolation within one hazard category; Substantially similar mixtures; and Aerosols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply bridging principles as found in paragraph A.0.5 of this Appendix to infer mixture classification from ingredient and similar-mixture data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of mixtures based on ingredient classifications when mixture data absent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no reliable evidence or test data for the specific mixture itself, and the bridging principles cannot be used... classification of the mixture is based on the classification of the ingredient substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixture shall be classified as a specific target organ toxicant when at least one ingredient has been classified as Category 1 or Category 2 and is present at or above the appropriate cut-off value/concentration limit specified in Table A.9.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-off/concentration limits for ingredient-triggered target organ toxicant classification (Table A.9.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ingredient classified as Category 1 Target organ toxicant or Category 2 Target organ toxicant: cut-off values/concentration limits triggering classification of a mixture as Category 1 or Category 2 are ≥1.0%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cut-off values and consequent classifications shall be applied equally and appropriately to both single- and repeated-dose target organ toxicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent classification for single- and repeated-dose target organ toxicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixtures shall be classified for either or both single- and repeated-dose toxicity independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and apply classification independently for single-exposure and repeated-exposure specific target organ toxicities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of potentiation and synergistic interactions in mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Care shall be exercised when toxicants affecting more than one organ system are combined that the potentiation or synergistic interactions are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain substances can cause specific target organ toxicity at <1% concentration when other ingredients in the mixture are known to potentiate its toxic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspiration hazard definition and general considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspiration hazard refers to severe acute effects such as chemical pneumonia, pulmonary injury or death occurring after aspiration of a substance or mixture; aspiration means the entry of a liquid or solid chemical directly through the oral or nasal cavity, or indirectly from vomiting, into the trachea and lower respiratory system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspiration is initiated at the moment of inspiration; aspiration via vomiting after ingestion has labeling implications (recommendation to induce vomiting may need modification if aspiration toxicity present).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of kinematic viscosity for aspiration classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification criteria refer to kinematic viscosity (conversion between dynamic and kinematic viscosity provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although definition includes solids, classification according to table A.10.1 for Category 1(b) is intended to apply to liquid substances and mixtures only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerosol/mist product considerations for aspiration hazard
rubrics_metrics.description: Aerosol and mist products classification shall be considered if their use may form a pool of product in the mouth which then may be aspirated; fine mists may not form a pool while streams or coarse mists may.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pump mechanism may be removed and contents available to be swallowed then classification of the products should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 1 aspiration criteria for substances (Table A.10.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A substance shall be classified in Category 1 for aspiration toxicity if (a) reliable and good quality human evidence indicates that it causes aspiration toxicity; or (b) if it is a hydrocarbon and has a kinematic viscosity ≤20.5 mm2/s, measured at 40 °C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of Category 1 substances include certain hydrocarbons, turpentine and pine oil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture classification Category 1 based on mixture data
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixture shall be classified in Category 1 based on reliable and good quality human evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mixture-level data are available and reliable, classify on the basis of those data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging/dilution threshold for aspiration toxicants in mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: For application of the dilution bridging principle, the concentration of aspiration toxicants shall not be less than 10%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bridging principles (dilution, batching, concentration, interpolation, substantially similar mixtures) for aspiration classification when mixture itself not tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'relevant ingredients' for mixture aspiration classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'relevant ingredients' of a mixture are those which are present in concentrations ≥1%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only ingredients ≥1% are considered relevant for the mixture-level calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture Category 1 aspiration quantitative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixture is classified as Category 1 when the sum of the concentrations of Category 1 ingredients is ≥10%, and the mixture has a kinematic viscosity of ≤20.5 mm2/s, measured at 40 °C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a mixture separates into distinct layers, the entire mixture is classified as Category 1 if any distinct layer meets the ≥10% sum of Category 1 ingredients and kinematic viscosity ≤20.5 mm2/s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explosive chemical definitions and class membership
rubrics_metrics.description: An explosive chemical is a solid or liquid capable by chemical reaction of producing gas at such temperature and pressure and at such speed as to cause damage; pyrotechnic chemicals and items are defined and included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explosive items, pyrotechnic items, unstable explosives, and intentional explosives are defined; class of explosives comprises explosive chemicals, explosive items, and chemicals/items manufactured with view to producing practical explosive or pyrotechnic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division-based classification for explosives (Divisions 1.1–1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemicals and items of this class shall be assigned to one of six divisions depending on the type of hazard they present: 1.1 mass explosion hazard; 1.2 projection hazard but not mass explosion; 1.3 fire hazard with minor blast/projection; 1.4 no significant hazard; 1.5 very insensitive with mass explosion hazard; 1.6 extremely insensitive items without mass explosion hazard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the definitions in B.1.2 to assign appropriate division based on hazard characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step explosive classification procedure and test series
rubrics_metrics.description: Explosives shall be classified as unstable explosives or assigned to divisions in accordance with the three step procedure in Part I of UN ST/SG/AC.10: (1) ascertain explosive effects (Test Series 1); (2) acceptance procedure (Test Series 2–4); (3) assignment to hazard division (Test Series 5–7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific additional tests (e.g., Series 8) determine inclusion of certain candidates (e.g., ANE) in oxidizing categories; see incorporated UN guidance and §1910.6 references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions: when a chemical is not classified as explosive
rubrics_metrics.description: A chemical is not classified as explosive if: (a) there are no chemical groups associated with explosive properties present in the molecule; or (b) the substance contains explosive-associated groups including oxygen and the calculated oxygen balance is less than −200; or (c) organic substance/exact mixture contains explosive groups but exothermic decomposition energy <500 J/g and onset <500 °C; or (d) for mixtures of inorganic oxidizing substances with organic material(s), oxidizer concentration below specified thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oxygen balance is calculated using the given formula: oxygen balance = −1600 [2x + (y/2) − z]/molecular weight. For inorganic oxidizers, concentration thresholds: <15% (Category 1/2) or <30% (Category 3) by mass may exclude classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flammable gas definition and special types
rubrics_metrics.description: Flammable gas means a gas having a flammable range with air at 20 °C and standard pressure; pyrophoric gas ignites spontaneously in air at ≤54 °C; chemically unstable gas can react explosively even without air/oxygen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions distinguish pyrophoric and chemically unstable gases for classification purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flammable gas category criteria (Table B.2.1: Categories 1A, 1B, 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 1A: gases ignitable at ≤13% by volume in air or having flammable range ≥12 percentage points; Category 1B: meet 1A flammability but are not pyrophoric/chemically unstable and have either a lower flammability limit >6% or fundamental burning velocity <10 cm/s; Category 2: gases other than 1A/1B with a flammable range at 20 °C/101.3 kPa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of data for Category 1B, a gas meeting 1A criteria shall by default be classified as 1A. Mixtures with >1% pyrophoric components shall be classified as pyrophoric unless data show otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional flammable gas classification considerations and test standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Flammability determined by tests or calculation in accordance with ISO 10156:1996 or ISO 10156:2017; burning velocity method per ISO 817 Annex C; pyrophoricity per IEC 60079-20-1 or DIN 51794:2003; chemical instability per UN ST/SG/AC.10 Part III.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where insufficient data exist, equivalent validated methods may be used and expert judgement can guide need for testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerosols classification criteria (Table B.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aerosols classified in three categories depending on flammable properties and heat of combustion: Category 1 contains ≥85% flammable components and heat ≥30 kJ/g or meets ignition distance/foam test criteria; Category 2 contains >1% flammable components or heat ≥20 kJ/g with specified ignition/enclosed-space/foam test criteria; Category 3 is 'does not meet 1 or 2' and contains ≤1% flammable components and heat <20 kJ/g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flammable components exclude pyrophoric, self-heating or water-reactive chemicals. If aerosols contain >1% flammable components or heat ≥20 kJ/g and not submitted for flammability procedures, classify as Category 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemicals under pressure definition and classification (Table B.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemicals under pressure are liquids or solids pressurized with gas at ≥200 kPa (gauge) at 20 °C in receptacles other than aerosol dispensers; they are classified into three categories based on flammable component content and heat of combustion: Category 1 (≥85% flammable components and heat ≥20 kJ/g), Category 2 (>1% and heat <20 kJ/g OR <85% and heat ≥20 kJ/g), Category 3 (≤1% and heat <20 kJ/g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flammable components do not include pyrophoric, self-heating or water-reactive substances; chemicals under pressure do not additionally fall within aerosols/gases under pressure/flammable liquids/solids categories but may fall within other hazard classes depending on contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerosol and chemicals-under-pressure additional data and heat of combustion calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: To classify an aerosol, data on flammable components, chemical heat of combustion and test results (aerosol foam flammability, ignition distance, enclosed space tests) are necessary. The chemical heat of combustion (ΔHc) in kJ/g is the product of theoretical heat of combustion and a combustion efficiency; for composite formulations, ΔHc(product) is the weighted sum of component ΔHc values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical heats of combustion shall be found in literature, calculated or determined by tests (see ASTM D240; ISO 13943; NFPA 30B) and relevant UN test subsections for ignition/enclosed-space/foam tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxidizing gas definition and single-category classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Oxidizing gas means any gas which may, generally by providing oxygen, cause or contribute to the combustion of other material more than air does (oxidizing power >23.5% by specified methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An oxidizing gas shall be classified in a single category for this class; classification in accordance with test/calculation methods described in ISO 10156 standards or equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gases under pressure definitions and grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Gases under pressure are gases contained at pressure ≥200 kPa (gauge) at 20 °C, or liquefied or refrigerated; groups: compressed gas, liquefied gas (high- and low-pressure distinctions by critical temperature), refrigerated liquefied gas, and dissolved gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical temperature thresholds define liquefied gas subtypes; aerosols should not be classified as gases under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flammable liquids category criteria (Table B.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flammable liquids classified in four categories by flash point and initial boiling point: Category 1: flash point <23 °C and initial boiling point ≤35 °C; Category 2: flash point <23 °C and initial boiling point >35 °C; Category 3: flash point ≥23 °C and ≤60 °C; Category 4: flash point >60 °C and ≤93 °C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flash point determined per specified ASTM methods or methods in GHS Rev 7; initial boiling point per ASTM D86-07a or ASTM D1078.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flammable solids definitions and burning-rate based classification (Table B.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flammable solid means a readily combustible solid or one that may cause/contribute to fire through friction; powdered/granular/pasty chemicals are classified using burning time/rate tests: burning time <45 s or rate >2.2 mm/s (or metal powder criteria) determine Category 1 vs Category 2 distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metal powders classified as flammable solids when ignitable and reaction spreads over whole sample in ≤10 min; solids causing fire through friction classified by analogy until definitive criteria established; tests per UN ST/SG/AC.10 Part III.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reactive chemicals definitions, exceptions, and types A–G
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-reactive chemicals are thermally unstable liquids or solids liable to strongly exothermic decomposition without oxygen; exclude explosives, organic peroxides, oxidizing liquids/solids except where mixtures meet criteria. Exclusions include heat of decomposition <300 J/g or SADT >75 °C for 50 kg package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify self-reactive chemicals into Types A–G based on laboratory behavior (detonation, deflagration, thermal explosion potential, effects when heated under confinement). Use test series A–H in UN ST/SG/AC.10 Part II and determine SADT per Part II section 28.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyrophoric liquid classification (ignite within 5 min)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pyrophoric liquid means a liquid liable to ignite within five minutes after coming into contact with air; Category 1: liquid ignites within 5 min when added to inert carrier and exposed to air or chars/ignites filter paper on contact within 5 min.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification procedure need not be applied when experience shows the chemical does not ignite spontaneously at normal temperatures (stable at room temp for prolonged periods). Tests per UN ST/SG/AC.10 Part III N.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyrophoric solid classification (ignite within 5 min)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pyrophoric solid means a solid liable to ignite within five minutes after coming into contact with air; Category 1: the solid ignites within 5 min of coming into contact with air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification of solid chemicals shall be based on tests performed on the chemical as presented; tests per UN ST/SG/AC.10 Part III N.2.
